2 Data and quality control

The data are whole-blood RNA-seq from GSE124326 (Krebs et al., 2020): 112 controls and 226 patients with bipolar I disorder, 152 taking lithium and 74 not taking it. Three groups give three networks. The prepared file holds log2-CPM values (genes x samples) and one row of metadata per sample, including sex, sequencing plate, and estimated blood-cell fractions.

course_data <- readRDS("data/gse124326_bd_lithium.rds")
expression_matrix <- course_data$expression   # genes x samples, log2-CPM
sample_info <- course_data$sample_info
stopifnot(identical(sample_info$sample, colnames(expression_matrix)))
dim(expression_matrix)

table(sample_info$treatment, sample_info$sex)
            
              F  M
  Control    67 45
  Lithium    90 62
  no Lithium 35 39
raw_variance <- apply(expression_matrix, 1, var)
top500 <- names(sort(raw_variance, decreasing = TRUE))[1:500]
pca <- prcomp(t(expression_matrix[top500, ]), scale. = TRUE)
pca_data <- cbind(sample_info, PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2])
pca_long <- pca_data |>
  select(PC1, PC2, treatment, sex, plate) |>
  pivot_longer(c(treatment, sex, plate), names_to = "variable", values_to = "level")
ggplot(pca_long, aes(PC1, PC2, color = level)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable) +
  labs(title = "PCA of the 500 most variable genes", color = NULL)

Sequencing plate drives PC1, the largest axis of variation. Sex barely shows on the first two PCs, even though XIST is the single most variable gene: one gene does not make a principal component. Lithium does not dominate the main axes either; its effect is real but small per gene. Plate and sex go into the limma model and are removed before building networks.

3 Gene selection

Network methods scale with the square of the number of genes, and genes that barely vary contribute mostly noise correlations. We first remove the plate and sex effects (keeping the group effects), keep expressed genes (mean log-CPM ≥ 2; at low counts, log values vary mostly by sampling noise), and then keep the 2,000 most variable of them. This filter ignores the condition labels, so later module–trait associations are not built in by the selection.

treatment_design <- model.matrix(~ factor(treatment, levels = grp_levels), data = sample_info)
adjusted_matrix <- limma::removeBatchEffect(
  expression_matrix, batch = sample_info$plate,
  covariates = model.matrix(~ sex, data = sample_info)[, -1, drop = FALSE],
  design = treatment_design)
expressed <- rowMeans(expression_matrix) >= 2   # drop low, noisy genes first
gene_variance <- apply(adjusted_matrix[expressed, ], 1, var)
selected_genes <- names(sort(gene_variance, decreasing = TRUE))[1:2000]
network_matrix <- adjusted_matrix[selected_genes, ]
dat_expr <- t(network_matrix)   # samples x genes for WGCNA and ARACNE
dim(dat_expr)
[1]  338 2000

c(before = rank_of(raw_variance, "XIST"), after = rank_of(___, "XIST"))

  1. Adjustment removes the female–male difference, so XIST loses most of its variance; it still varies between women and may stay in the top 2,000.
  2. The random genes correlate more, and the first PC of both sets follows the neutrophil fraction (a PC’s sign is arbitrary, so read |r|). In whole blood, the mix of cell types moves thousands of genes up and down together. Strong correlation is not automatically interesting structure: ask what drives it. That cell-mix axis is also why the lithium contrast, which raises neutrophils, needs care.

4 Differential expression with limma

limma tests all expressed genes, with sex and plate as covariates. One model answers two questions: lithium (on vs off lithium, within bipolar disorder) and diagnosis (patients off lithium vs controls, so the drug does not leak into the disease contrast). trend = TRUE lets the prior variance follow mean expression, as recommended for log-CPM data.

group_factor <- factor(sample_info$treatment, levels = grp_levels)
design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + group_factor + sex + plate, data = sample_info)
colnames(design) <- make.names(sub("group_factor", "", colnames(design)))
contrasts <- limma::makeContrasts(lithium = Lithium - no.Lithium,
                                  diagnosis = no.Lithium - Control, levels = design)
fit <- limma::lmFit(expression_matrix, design)
fit <- limma::eBayes(limma::contrasts.fit(fit, contrasts), trend = TRUE)
limma_results <- limma::topTable(fit, coef = "lithium", number = Inf)       # BH
diagnosis_results <- limma::topTable(fit, coef = "diagnosis", number = Inf)
head(limma_results)

  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#5E4E56", `TRUE` = pal$rose),

  labs(title = "Lithium vs no lithium (adjusted for sex and plate)", color = NULL)

Thousands of genes pass FDR for lithium, but few change by more than ~1.4-fold: with 338 samples, small shifts are detectable. The diagnosis contrast finds fewer. Leaving out sex and plate adds noise and changes the answer. DEGs are under-represented among the most variable genes (28% of the network genes vs 38% genome-wide): in blood, variance is dominated by differences between people (HLA genotype, cell mix), not by lithium. We come back to this overlap at the end.

  <dbl>   <int>      <int>
1    12      12        172

The power changes the partition: here β = 6 gives 10 modules and 231 grey genes, against 12 and 172 at β = 12. A lower power keeps more weak correlations, so the topological overlap is flatter and branch boundaries in the tree shift. Module boundaries are a choice, so report them.

TipExercise 6 · Do ARACNE hubs and WGCNA hubs agree?

Take the 50 genes with the highest ARACNE degree. Which WGCNA modules do they belong to? How many of the trait-associated module’s top-50 kME genes are also ARACNE hubs?

aracne_hubs <- names(sort(aracne_degree, decreasing = TRUE))[1:___]
table(module_colors[aracne_hubs])
kme_top50 <- names(head(sort(kme_mod, decreasing = TRUE), 50))  # whole module if smaller

NoteShow solution 
aracne_hubs <- names(sort(aracne_degree, decreasing = TRUE))[1:50]
table(module_colors[aracne_hubs])

    black      blue     brown     green      grey   magenta       red       tan 
        4        12         6         3         4         3         2         1 
turquoise    yellow 
       11         4 
kme_top50 <- names(head(sort(kme_mod, decreasing = TRUE), 50))  # whole module if smaller
length(intersect(aracne_hubs, kme_top50))
[1] 4

Here 4 genes are hubs in both. The two methods define importance differently: a WGCNA hub sits at the centre of one module, while ARACNE’s pruning removes indirect links, so its hubs are genes with many direct, non-redundant partners, often bridging modules (look at the module table above). Little overlap is common; genes found by both are the more robust candidates.

7 wTO networks per group

wTO is computed separately for each group (controls, patients off lithium, patients on lithium) on all 2,000 genes with 100 bootstrap resamples. The p-value measures stability: the share of resamples in which a link moved by more than delta = 0.2.

wto_nets <- load_wto_networks(network_matrix, sample_info, n = 100)
sapply(wto_nets[c("control", "no_lithium", "lithium")],
       function(x) sum(x$pval.adj < 0.05))   # stable links per group
   control no_lithium    lithium 
   1868928    1244632    1955501

Sign flips are the raw material of CoDiNA’s β class. Lithium was not randomized, so treat them as hypotheses.

8 Consensus network

A consensus asks which links are robust across related networks. Patients off and on lithium share the disease and differ in treatment, so their consensus is a bipolar-disorder network that does not depend on lithium.

as_wto_input <- function(x) data.frame(Node.1 = factor(x$Node.1), Node.2 = factor(x$Node.2),
                                       wTO = x$wTO, pval = x$pval)
consensus <- wTO::wTO.Consensus(list(as_wto_input(wto_nets$no_lithium),
                                     as_wto_input(wto_nets$lithium)))

TipExercise 8 · The bipolar consensus

Keep links with |CN| ≥ 0.3 and a BH-adjusted Fisher p < 0.05 (on 2,000 genes, wTO rarely exceeds 0.4). How many are there? How many of them are strong (|ω| ≥ 0.3) and same-signed in both patient groups, and how many are carried by only one?

  mutate(padj = p.adjust(pval.fisher, "BH")) |>
  filter(abs(CN) >= ___, padj < ___)
ab <- inner_join(wto_nets$no_lithium, wto_nets$lithium,
                 by = c("Node.1", "Node.2"), suffix = c(".off", ".on")) |>
  semi_join(robust |> mutate(across(c(Node.1, Node.2), as.character)),
            by = c("Node.1", "Node.2"))
table(agrees = sign(ab$wTO.off) == sign(ab$wTO.on) &
        pmin(abs(ab$wTO.off), abs(ab$wTO.on)) >= ___)

ggplot(ab |> slice_sample(n = min(8000, nrow(ab))), aes(wTO.off, wTO.on, color = agrees)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pal$rose, `TRUE` = pal$gold),
                     labels = c("carried by one group", "agrees in both")) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Bipolar consensus links: off vs on lithium",
       x = "wTO · no Lithium", y = "wTO · Lithium", color = NULL)

Weighting by |ω| lets the stronger network dominate: a link that is strong in one group and weak in the other still gets a large CN and a small Fisher p. Always check per-network agreement. The links that agree form the shared bipolar network; the ones carried by one group are where CoDiNA looks for treatment effects.

9 CoDiNA

With three networks, every link is a point in the cube \([-1,1]^3\) and its class says where it is present: g.noLithium.Lithium = both patient groups but not controls (disease), g.Lithium = only on lithium, and so on.

to_codina <- function(x, padj = 0.05) {
  x |> filter(pval.adj < padj) |> transmute(Node.1, Node.2, wTO)
}
codina_input <- lapply(wto_nets[c("control", "no_lithium", "lithium")], to_codina)
codes <- c("Control", "noLithium", "Lithium")
codina_result <- CoDiNA::MakeDiffNet(Data = codina_input, Code = codes,
                                     cutoff = 0.33, stretch = TRUE)
sort(table(codina_result$Phi_tilde), decreasing = TRUE)

                  a   g.Control.Lithium           g.Lithium g.noLithium.Lithium 
             484941              164255              147171              112864 
        g.noLithium           g.Control g.Control.noLithium b.noLithium.Lithium 
             111694              101222               42568                  16 
        b.noLithium 
                  4
TipExercise 9 · Why stretch?

The three networks come from 112, 74 and 152 samples. Compare their |wTO| distributions, then re-run MakeDiffNet() with stretch = FALSE. How do the γ classes change, and why?

sapply(wto_nets[c("control", "no_lithium", "lithium")],
       function(x) quantile(abs(x$wTO), ___))
codina_raw <- CoDiNA::MakeDiffNet(Data = codina_input, Code = codes,
                                  cutoff = 0.33, stretch = ___)
sort(table(codina_raw$Phi_tilde), decreasing = TRUE)
NoteShow solution 
sapply(wto_nets[c("control", "no_lithium", "lithium")],
       function(x) quantile(abs(x$wTO), c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99)))
    control no_lithium lithium
50%   0.138      0.166   0.145
90%   0.311      0.341   0.308
99%   0.428      0.433   0.408
codina_raw <- CoDiNA::MakeDiffNet(Data = codina_input, Code = codes,
                                  cutoff = 0.33, stretch = FALSE)
full_join(as.data.frame(table(Phi_tilde = codina_result$Phi_tilde)),
          as.data.frame(table(Phi_tilde = codina_raw$Phi_tilde)),
          by = "Phi_tilde", suffix = c(".stretch", ".raw"))
            Phi_tilde Freq.stretch Freq.raw
1                   a       484941    90802
2         b.noLithium            4       NA
3 b.noLithium.Lithium           16       NA
4           g.Control       101222    24664
5   g.Control.Lithium       164255    13639
6 g.Control.noLithium        42568    22926
7           g.Lithium       147171    13091
8         g.noLithium       111694    87739
9 g.noLithium.Lithium       112864    19994

The networks do not share one scale: the 74-patient network sits highest across its whole |wTO| distribution. On the raw scale, links cross the 0.33 threshold most often in that group, so the γ links pile up in g.noLithium and most other classes shrink. stretch = TRUE rescales each network by its own maximum |wTO| before discretizing. Group size is one reason for the different scales (correlations from fewer samples are noisier, and noise inflates |r|); real differences in co-expression are another. A stricter check is to subsample every group to the same size and rebuild the networks.

 [1] "ADISSP"    "ALDH2"     "ATP9A"     "BUB1"      "C14orf132" "CAPN12"

[13] "FAT4"      "FCN1"      "FCRL5"

ClusterNodes() counts each gene’s links per class and keeps the class only when a chi-square test says the links concentrate there (BH < 0.05); otherwise the gene is “U” (unclassified). Disease genes are connected in both patient groups but not in controls, so lithium cannot explain them; lithium-only genes gain partners only in treated patients.

TipExercise 11 · The background matters

Run GO Biological Process ORA on the lithium-only (g.Lithium) genes twice: once with the 2,000 network genes as universe, once without a universe (whole annotated genome). Compare the number of terms with FDR < 0.05.

to_entrez <- function(symbols) clusterProfiler::bitr(
  symbols, fromType = "SYMBOL", toType = "ENTREZID", OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db)
ora <- function(genes, universe = NULL) clusterProfiler::enrichGO(
  gene = unique(to_entrez(genes)$ENTREZID),
  universe = if (is.null(universe)) NULL else unique(to_entrez(universe)$ENTREZID),
  OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db, keyType = "ENTREZID", ont = "BP",
  pAdjustMethod = "BH", pvalueCutoff = 1, qvalueCutoff = 1)
sum(as.data.frame(ora(case_genes, ___))$p.adjust < 0.05)

The two runs ask different questions. Against the 2,000 network genes: are the g.Lithium genes special among variable blood genes? Against the whole genome: are they special among all annotated genes? The genome background adds thousands of genes and tests, so terms can appear or disappear in either direction. Always report the universe you used.
